sources.summary: President Donald Trump attended the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association Dinner Friday night.
sources.articleSummary: Trump began his remarks reflecting on the earlier event disrupted by gunfire. President Donald Trump addressed reporters and other guests Friday at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner, which was rescheduled after ending abruptly three months ago when shots rang out, seesawing from a tone of working together with the press to lobbing insults against his political opponents and some journalists. The speech, which lasted more than an hour and received an at-times muted response from the attendees, ended with the president donning a red cap reading "Trump 2028" after joking that he was running for another term, which is barred by the Constitution. President Donald Trump speaks during the 2026 White House Correspondents' Association Dinner at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington, July 24, 2026. Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images "As I said three months ago, the show must go on," Trump said at the top of his remarks. "Tonight we come back together to answer that heinous attack with unwavering resolve," to show that "in America we do not yield to political violence," Trump said. Trump said his speech planned for the initial dinner was "going to be a doozy." "I was so psyched. I was going to rip people, and I don't know. Just something changed," Trump said. "It's really for the better, but I just wouldn't want to do that. But we'll do a little ripping if you don't mind." Trump touched on his White House ballroom and other projects, defended the war in Iran and even offered some praise for the work of the White House press corps. "I have tremendous respect for the people in this room," Trump said. "Sometimes I don't feel you treat me fair. I don't feel that, but sometimes you treat me very fairly, and I have a lot of respect for your profession." But Trump also criticized some reporters by name and also attacked his frequent Democratic targets -- including former President Joe Biden, Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer, California Gov. Elizabeth Warren and California Sen. Adam Schiff -- often using offensive nicknames. Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo At the end of his speech, the president whipped out a "Trump 2028" hat as he jokingly announced, in a "scoop" for the crowd, his intention to run for another term, before thanking those in the room for having the courage to be there. "Most of us went through a period of trauma from just a short while ago, and you know, some people said they wanted to come, but they were afraid to come, and you people weren't afraid to come," Trump said. Ahead of the event, the White House promised that the president's speech would be "unifying yet vicious." "The president's speech will be a combination of unifying yet vicious, and serious yet hilarious, all at the same time, if you can imagine that. One thing I can assure you, it will be entertaining," White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement to ABC News on Friday ahead of the event. The dinner in April devolved into chaos after authorities say Cole Allen opened fire inside the Washington Hilton hotel, where thousands of journalists and guests gathered for the annual celebration of the First Amendment.

failureClasses.label: Language integrity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any incomplete sentence, clipped word, mojibake, spelling/grammar failure, copied/noisy source fragment, or dangling phrase regardless of the exact word involved.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Clean or remove the defective sentence, rebuild missing context from dossier facts, normalize encoding, then resubmit the same article.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Run language-integrity checks on every paragraph before validation, not just against previously seen bad words.

failureClasses.label: Originality/public-copy failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any repeated sentence pattern, summary/body duplication, generic template language, or behind-the-scenes process language.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Rewrite summary and transitions in public-facing language, remove backend/process phrasing, vary sentence structure, then resubmit.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Before Editor review, compare summary/body/transition phrasing against recent CE output and forbidden process-language classes.

failureClasses.label: Evidence depth failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any draft that lacks enough verified facts, context, source diversity, or intro/body/ending structure for its publication tier.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Return to source evidence and dossier facts, add verified context, and regenerate only the weak sections.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Writer must prove it used a complete Story Dossier before first sentence generation.

failureClasses.label: Story identity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any paragraph, headline, source, or summary whose primary actor/event differs from the Story Dossier event.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Split mixed clusters, remove off-event source fragments, rebuild the dossier around one canonical event, then rewrite affected sections.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Require every draft paragraph to map to the same event id or an explicit dossier relationship before the Writer proceeds.

Yemen's Houthis announce strikes on Aramco oil facilities in Saudi Arabia The Houthis, an Iran-backed paramilitary group in Yemen, announced strikes on Saudi oil company Aramco's facilities in Jizan and Yanbu on Saturday. The Houthis fired "dozens of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones," which successfully hit their targets, according to spokesperson Yahya Saree. The strikes or whether they were successful could not be independently verified. The group also confirmed the military blockade of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern exit point of the Red Sea, remains in effect. The Houthis struck two Saudi-flagged commercial tankers in the Red Sea earlier this week, but had not struck any ships since then, bringing some calm to the region. "We will not hesitate to expand our operations and escalate our actions based on developments in the coming hours and days, within the equation of a blockade for a blockade and an escalation for an escalation," Saree said in a statement. https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-us-trump-strait-hormuz-middle-east/#post-update-84edbf2b link copied Ukraine targets vessel carrying military shipments to Iran, Zelenskyy says The two major ongoing wars crossed paths on Saturday when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced his country had struck a ship carrying arms for Iran. As has become usual, the president ran off a list of long-distance strikes inside Russia, including targeting a weapons plant in Kirov, oil refinery in Tyumen and a logistics facility in Yekaterinburg, among others. But he also mentioned an unusual strike. "We also achieved very strong results with long‐range strikes in the Caspian Sea - including vessels used in military cargo shipments involving Iran, as well as a warship," Zelenskyy said on X. It's unclear what the ship might have been carrying to Iran, but Russia is a close ally of the Iranians and vice versa. Iran had provided many Shahed attack drones to Russia in the first couple years of the war, until Iran needed more for their own use of late. Just yesterday in a Truth Social post, the president claimed he does not believe Russia or China are selling weapons to Iran, writing "two major Countries that people speak of often in terms of Iran are, in my opinion, not participating. If they did, it would be very bad for them - Certainly not in their best interests." Iran reports no strikes overnight for the first time in almost 2 weeks Iran reported no strikes overnight into Saturday, an apparent break from nearly two weeks of consecutive nights of U.S. attacks, but tensions remain high in the region.

The event was moved to the Waldorf Astoria and had about a quarter of the attendees of the event in April, which was interrupted when a gunman attempted to enter the ballroom and attack officials. President Trump appeared at the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association Dinner, which took place in Washington, D.C. on Friday with a new location and a drastically reduced list of attendees, following the cancellation of the event in April after a gunman fired shots as the event was underway. Moved to the Waldorf Astoria in the nation's capital instead of the Washington Hilton and reduced from 2,600 guests down to around 680, it was less a star-studded event that each year sees celebrity guests brush elbows with reporters and editors as they sit with the politicians they cover - the optics of which are criticized each year by journalists and For the make-up dinner, the WHCA is also bringing back the Secret Service member who survived the April shooting, when 31-year-old Cole Tomas Allen, who allegedly intended to target multiple Trump administration officials, was arrested near the screening area outside the banquet hall after running past the security checkpoint. The awards were handed out; mentalist Oz Pearlman, who got just one private trick for the White House press secretary at the first dinner before gunshots caused chaos, returned to deliver some levity; and ahead of the event, a group of hundreds of former journalists and press freedom groups sent a letter to the WHCA. The president took to the stage around 9:30 p.m. ET and brought up the attempted attack early in his much-anticipated speech, which has been speculated upon heavily in April and again ahead of the July event.

sources.title: ‘Cockroaches won’: India’s education minister resigns amid massive youth protests
sources.summary: India’s education minister resigned Saturday after escalating nationwide “Cockroach” demonstrations and an activist’s 26-day hunger strike demanding his resignation.
sources.articleSummary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters celebrate the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on July 25. Arun Sankar / AFP via Getty Images Share Add NBC News to Google July 25, 2026, 6:42 AM EDT By Freddie Clayton India’s education minister resigned Saturday after escalating nationwide “Cockroach” demonstrations and an activist’s 26-day hunger strike demanding his resignation. Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content. Dharmendra Pradhan announced his resignation on X hours before a third round of talks was set to begin between the government and an activist movement, the Cockroach Janta Party, which has demanded major reforms after the handling of an alleged exam paper leak triggered one of India’s biggest displays of public dissent in recent years. “I hold deep respect for the aspirations, sentiments, and rightful expectations of the youth of this country,” Pradhan wrote on X. “Realising the dreams of India’s young generation has been the moral resolve of our political and social life.” “Cockroaches won. Democracy won!” the CJP, a viral movement that began as an online parody of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), said in a post on X. In New Delhi, crowds of students and activists were celebrating in the streets following the announcement, many of them waving India flags. The scandal has been growing since May, when online leaks disrupted the NEET undergraduate exam, the fiercely competitive gateway to India’s medical schools. Sajjad Hussain / AFP via Getty Images Anger among India’s young people has exploded onto the streets in recent weeks, with protests spreading from New Delhi to other cities around the country, including Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Ahmedabad. Authorities have struggled to contain the growing protests, with police deploying tear gas and batons against the vast crowds close to the country’s Parliament building in New Delhi earlier this week. The CJP, named after a remark from India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant comparing unemployed young people to “cockroaches,” has been at the centre of what has become the biggest challenge to Modi in his 12 years in power. As well as the minister’s resignation, protesters’ demands included compensation for the families of students who died by suicide after the exam paper leaks, and accountability over police suppression of their protests. “The families of the children who committed suicide should receive compensation” of one crore rupees ($100,000), CJP posted Saturday. “And second, these police goons who acted on the 20th. Action must be taken against the police officers for that.” On Thursday night, Modi offered his first public comments in a video posted to Instagram. “I know the paper leak is not a trivial matter,” he said, announcing fast-track courts to prosecute cases involving examination paper leaks, while defending his government’s handling of the scandal.

sources.title: India education minister resigns after weeks of "Cockroach" protests
sources.summary: India's education minister resigned Saturday after weeks of protests that demanded his removal over irregularities in the education system.
sources.articleSummary: India's education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday after weeks of protests that demanded his removal over alleged leaks in some of the country's most competitive entrance exams and irregularities in the education system. Pradhan announced the decision in a post on X, handing a major victory to the "Cockroach" movement, which has spearheaded nationwide demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes. His resignation also marks the first significant concession by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government to one of the most visible waves of public dissent it has faced in recent years. The movement began more than a month ago after allegations of leaks in some of India's biggest entrance exams. It started as a call for education reforms but has grown into a broader protest over unemployment, government accountability and economic opportunities. Students, professionals, families and activists have joined rallies in New Delhi and other cities across India. News of Pradhan's resignation sparked celebrations among the thousands of protesters who have camped at New Delhi's protest site for more than a month. Many embraced each other and waved the Indian flag. Prachi Kumar, a corporate employee who joined the protests, said Pradhan's resignation was necessary to restore accountability in the education system. Someone must be held accountable," she said. The Cockroach Janta Party, which launched the protest movement, declared victory following the resignation, writing on X: "DEMOCRACY WINS!" The demonstrations have become one of the most persistent challenges to Modi's government in recent years, with thousands returning to the streets even after police used tear gas and batons to disperse marchers. Tensions escalated on Monday when police moved to disperse thousands of protesters marching toward Parliament. Several students were injured in the crackdown, intensifying anger among demonstrators. Modi's government had earlier sought to ease tensions by announcing fast-track courts for cases involving exam paper leaks and saying it would introduce legislation to strengthen measures against cheating and corruption in the examination system. The measures failed to satisfy protesters, who said they did not address government accountability. Although Pradhan's resignation met their main demand, the movement leaders said their campaign would continue as they sought compensation for families of students who died by suicide after alleged exam paper leaks and action against police officers they accused of using excessive force. "Remember, do not mess with (the) cockroach," Abhijeet Dipke, a movement leader, said in a written statement. storySnapshot.originalHeadline: Troy Jackson: the Maine lumberjack Democrats believe can beat Susan Collins
storySnapshot.articleSummary: Jackson, set to replace Graham Platner, is prominent workers’ rights advocate and a leading progressive voice As cinemagoers flock to The Odyssey, Democrats in Maine are. Troy Jackson: the Maine lumberjack Democrats believe can beat Susan Collins. BANGOR, Maine — Former state Senate President Troy Jackson is on the cusp of becoming Democrats’ Senate nominee in Maine, starting a 101-day sprint to Election Day in a n. Maine Democrats are gathering Saturday for the party's nominating convention to select a U.S. Senate nominee to replace Graham Platner on the ballot in November, with former state Senate President Troy Jackson poised to secure the nomination. They are set to nominate lumberjack Troy Jackson this weekend as their candidate to challenge Susan Collins, a veteran Republican in the US Senate, after the implosion of the party’s original candidate left them scrambling for a replacement less than four months before the midterm elections. While Kamala Harris infamously had only 107 days to build a presidential campaign in 2024, Jackson would have even less time for a battle that could decide control of the 100-member Senate. Hundreds of Democrats are gathering in Bangor on Saturday morning for a state convention to pick their Senate nominee after the primary winner, Graham Platner, ended his campaign earlier this month after a sexual assault allegation, which he denied. Susan Collins, the only Republican representing a state President Donald Trump lost in 2024, is seeking a sixth term. Democrats are looking to net four seats and take control of the Senate this fall, and Maine represents one of their best opportunities to notch a win, at least on paper. sources.articleSummary: Troy Jackson at an event in Portland, Maine, in May. Jackson is set to be nominated at a special convention on Saturday. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Democrats Profile Troy Jackson: the Maine lumberjack Democrats believe can beat Susan Collins Jackson, set to replace Graham Platner, is prominent workers’ rights advocate and a leading progressive voice As cinemagoers flock to The Odyssey, Democrats in Maine are hoping that their long and perilous quest for a political hero ends in Troy. They are set to nominate lumberjack Troy Jackson this weekend as their candidate to challenge Susan Collins, a veteran Republican in the US Senate, after the implosion of the party’s original candidate left them scrambling for a replacement less than four months before the midterm elections. Jackson, a former president of the Democratic-controlled Maine senate, is widely expected to secure the nomination at a special party convention in Bangor on Saturday. He would inherit a race transformed by the abrupt withdrawal of the primary winner, Graham Platner, following allegations of sexual assault made by a former girlfriend, accusations he has denied. While Kamala Harris infamously had only 107 days to build a presidential campaign in 2024, Jackson would have even less time for a battle that could decide control of the 100-member Senate. The fifth-generation logger from Aroostook county in northern Maine combines an unusual political biography with an unapologetically progressive platform. He first came to prominence in the late 1990s when he led a week-long blockade by Maine loggers protesting the employment of Canadian workers, whom they accused of depressing wages. The demonstration ended with police escorting him away but established his reputation as a champion of rural workers, which would continue into his time as a legislator. Jackson initially ran as a Republican in 2000 when he sought a seat in Maine’s house of representatives. He lost but won two years later when he ran as an independent. He switched to the Democratic party in 2004 and went on to serve three terms in the house before being elected to the state senate, where he was president from 2018 until 2024. View image in fullscreen Jackson with fellow loggers at a protest at the US-Canada border in October 1998. Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/AP In contrast to Platner, the biggest scandal attached to him so far is that he displayed flashes of temper such as cursing, shouting and throwing a water bottle in a meeting when he could not persuade someone to vote his way, according to a Washington Post report based on interviews with more than two dozen people. Jackson’s political views have shifted significantly over the years. Earlier in his career he opposed abortion rights and same-sex marriage, positions he has since abandoned. He has emerged as one of Maine’s leading progressives, backing policies such as Medicare for All and calling for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). For those seeking an economic populist and working-class champion, he appears to fit the bill.

sources.articleSummary: Lou Koller, the founding frontman of New York hardcore institution Sick of It All, has died following a battle with esophageal cancer. The band confirmed his death in a statement posted to Instagram on Friday (July 24). “It’s with unbelievable sadness that we announce to our worldwide hardcore family the passing of our brother Lou Koller,” the group wrote, noting that 2026 would have marked the band’s 40th anniversary. “We have lost a beloved friend and an iconic frontman. Lou had the power to raise everyone’s spirits at our shows with a smile and a sarcastic comment, and he won people over wherever we played, from every culture and every corner of the world.” The band also thanked those who had contributed to Koller’s medical fund, writing that his “battle is over now Koller first revealed his diagnosis in the summer of 2024, telling fans that doctors had found a tumor in his esophagus that extended into his stomach. Sick of It All cancelled a European tour so he could undergo treatment, and the hardcore community rallied with benefit concerts and donations. By May 2025, he had announced he was cancer-free following a final round of chemotherapy, but the disease returned months later. Sick of It All formed in Queens, New York in 1986, built around Koller and his brother Pete, the band’s guitarist.

Discovery has filed a lawsuit against Amazon, accusing it of "inducing contracted employees to breach their employment agreements." In its complaint, the company said Amazon "openly embarked upon an unlawful course" and hurriedly tried to "pirate away a number of contracted employees" across its subsidiaries. But what seemed to have compelled Warner Bros. to sue Amazon was the poaching of Pia Barlow, the former EVP for originals marketing at HBO Max. Barlow's contract wasn't set to expire until October 31, 2027, the lawsuit reads, and the company said she committed to stay with Warner Bros. Amazon, which was apparently aware of her contract, offer her a higher pay package that she then accepted. Barlow left HBO Max 16 months before her contract was slated to end and is expected to start working at Amazon on August 3. has also accused Amazon of promising to pay for Barlow's legal representation if she was ever sued for breach of contract. The complaint also mentions how Amazon allegedly tried to induce another Warner Bros. employee to breach their term of agreement before it was set to expire in December 2027. In that case, though, Amazon was ultimately unsuccessful. According to Deadline, the other employee was most likely Francesca Orsi, the EVP for HBO Programming and head of HBO Drama Series and Films. Amazon reportedly tried to get her to lead its Drama and Comedy department. When she didn't sign on, the company instead named three different heads for Drama, Comedy and Young Adult. Discover is suing Amazon for intentional interference with contractual relations, inducing breach of contract, intentional interference with prospective economic advantage and unfair competition. It's now asking the court for a preliminary and permanent injunction preventing Amazon from inducing breach of contract with its employees, as well as for an unspecified amount of monetary compensation for damages.

sources.articleSummary: The Trump administration conceded that it canceled 284 grants from states that voted against President Donald Trump in the 2024 election. David Ake / Getty Images file Share Add NBC News to Google July 24, 2026, 6:12 PM EDT By Gary Grumbach and Kyla Guilfoil The Trump administration admitted that it terminated nearly 300 federal research grants “solely because” the projects were connected to states that voted against President Donald Trump in 2024 and had two Democratic senators in office, according to court filings. Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content. The administration made the admission in a court filing this month responding to a lawsuit brought by University of California researchers challenging the cancellation. In the filing, the administration wrote as an undisputed statement of fact that on a list of more than 2,300 financial assistance awards across the Department of Energy, 624 grants on these lists were designated either “termination” or “cancel.” Of those 624 grants, Jeff Novak, the principal deputy general counsel of the Department of Energy, wrote that in October 2025 the Office of Management and Budget identified 284 specific grants that were marked to be terminated. Novak wrote that with one exception, “the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing Senators.” Novak added that the remaining 340 grants proposed for termination were ultimately not canceled in October 2025 nor since then. “All such grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election or has at least one Republican-caucusing Senator,” Novak wrote of the unterminated grants. Novak wrote that the decision to cancel the grants listed in the October notice tranche — those 284 — was not “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor.” “DOE accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, i.e., whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State,” Novak wrote. He added that the Department of Energy “will not contend that it looked beyond the prime grantee(s) to consider the political identity or geographic distribution of downstream beneficiaries of the grant funds.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Department of Energy argued in a statement Friday that court filings did not show that termination decisions were made on a political basis. “That is a misrepresentation of the court filing and of Mr. Novak’s words,” Ben Dietderich, press secretary for the Energy Department, said in a statement. “None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations.

sources.title: Cathy Engelbert helped the WNBA capitalize on growth, but now her relationship with players is holding it back
sources.summary: At WNBA All-Star Weekend in Chicago, players spoke about a relationship with the commissioner that is overdue for change
sources.articleSummary: CHICAGO -- WNBA All-Star Weekend has grown so much over the past few years that two-time MVP Elena Delle Donne, who made her first of seven All-Star Games in 2013, hardly recognized it when she paused her retirement to participate in the WNBA Shooting Stars competition on Friday night. "This All-Star looks a little bit different than the first one," she said after her team won the inaugural event, which paired an active player with a legend and a high-school star. "My first one, it was almost like just like pulling up for a scrimmage and leaving. Now it's like a whole weekend, and everybody is getting celebrated the way they should. It's a place everybody wants to be to show up and have fun together." Most of that growth has taken place under the leadership of Cathy Engelbert, who became the WNBA's first commissioner (prior to her hiring, the league only had presidents) on July 17, 2019. Engelbert has helped shepherd the league from a budget-sheet afterthought and annoyance to NBA owners into a billion-dollar behemoth that has NBA owners fighting over who gets to pay upward of $250 million to launch the next team. This spring, the league and union signed a landmark CBA that saw player salaries increase by almost 400%. This is the WNBA's 30th anniversary season, and this All-Star Weekend in Chicago was supposed to be a chance for all parties to come together, soak in the success and riches, take a shot with the StudBudz and give all the league's skeptics over the years a nice fat "told you so." But instead, for the second season in a row, the league's marquee event has been overshadowed by conflict between the league's front office and players. Last year, players took the court before the All-Star Game wearing shirts that said, "Pay Us What You Owe Us" -- signaling their resolve in the then-upcoming CBA negotiations and frustration that Engelbert and WNBA owners were not taking them seriously. It wasn't a great look for the league, but a little discord and tension during a contract year is to be expected. This year, the conflict is much more self-inflicted. The weeks leading up to All-Star have been marred by missteps and miscommunications, and one of the biggest questions lingering over media day on Friday was whether Engelbert should remain at the helm. And while players met with Engelbert about pressing issues on Tuesday night and took a measured tone with media -- WNBPA president Nneka Ogwumike expressed sympathy for Engelbert and said it wasn't for her to decide whether she should remain at her post -- at a certain point, if you have to ask the question, you might already know the answer. Engelbert has helped forever change the trajectory of the WNBA and women's sports as a whole, and I believe that if she steps aside soon, history will remember her tenure fondly. sourcePool.articleSummary: CHICAGO -- WNBA All-Star Weekend has grown so much over the past few years that two-time MVP Elena Delle Donne, who made her first of seven All-Star Games in 2013, hardly recognized it when she paused her retirement to participate in the WNBA Shooting Stars competition on Friday night. "This All-Star looks a little bit different than the first one," she said after her team won the inaugural event, which paired an active player with a legend and a high-school star. "My first one, it was almost like just like pulling up for a scrimmage and leaving. Now it's like a whole weekend, and everybody is getting celebrated the way they should. It's a place everybody wants to be to show up and have fun together." Most of that growth has taken place under the leadership of Cathy Engelbert, who became the WNBA's first commissioner (prior to her hiring, the league only had presidents) on July 17, 2019. Engelbert has helped shepherd the league from a budget-sheet afterthought and annoyance to NBA owners into a billion-dollar behemoth that has NBA owners fighting over who gets to pay upward of $250 million to launch the next team. This spring, the league and union signed a landmark CBA that saw player salaries increase by almost 400%. This is the WNBA's 30th anniversary season, and this All-Star Weekend in Chicago was supposed to be a chance for all parties to come together, soak in the success and riches, take a shot with the StudBudz and give all the league's skeptics over the years a nice fat "told you so." But instead, for the second season in a row, the league's marquee event has been overshadowed by conflict between the league's front office and players. Last year, players took the court before the All-Star Game wearing shirts that said, "Pay Us What You Owe Us" -- signaling their resolve in the then-upcoming CBA negotiations and frustration that Engelbert and WNBA owners were not taking them seriously. It wasn't a great look for the league, but a little discord and tension during a contract year is to be expected. This year, the conflict is much more self-inflicted. The weeks leading up to All-Star have been marred by missteps and miscommunications, and one of the biggest questions lingering over media day on Friday was whether Engelbert should remain at the helm. And while players met with Engelbert about pressing issues on Tuesday night and took a measured tone with media -- WNBPA president Nneka Ogwumike expressed sympathy for Engelbert and said it wasn't for her to decide whether she should remain at her post -- at a certain point, if you have to ask the question, you might already know the answer. Engelbert has helped forever change the trajectory of the WNBA and women's sports as a whole, and I believe that if she steps aside soon, history will remember her tenure fondly. But while busy activating brands and holding bottom lines, Engelbert has overlooked other important parts of her job, such as building relationships with the fans, the media and, most importantly, the players. "Show us that you hear us, that you're there for us, and then we go from there," A'ja Wilson said on Friday, when asked for her thoughts on WNBA leadership.

storySnapshot.originalHeadline: ‘Nobody was there for us’: mother urges Andy Burnham to reopen case of daughter killed in Texas
storySnapshot.summary: Photograph: Jane Coates That Christmas, Lucy and her boyfriend, Sam Littler, flew to Texas to spend time with her father, Kris Harrison, who had left the family home when she was two.
storySnapshot.articleSummary: Lucy Harrison, 23, was shot in 2025 with her father’s gun. He was never arrested and a grand jury chose not to indict him Lucy Harrison felt that 2024 was her best year y. ‘Nobody was there for us’: mother urges Andy Burnham to reopen case of daughter killed in Texas. The 23-year-old had graduated from university with first class honours, landed her dream job and bought her first house with her boyfriend. She was a “big girl adult” now, Lucy would say. She shed tears of joy seeing her idol, Taylor Swift, at Wembley on the Eras tour that summer. “All the hard work, all the tears, everything was coming to fruition,” said her mother, Jane Coates, from Warrington in north-west England. View image in fullscreen Jane Coates, pictured here with Lucy for the final time, raised her daughter alone from the age of two. Photograph: Jane Coates That Christmas, Lucy and her boyfriend, Sam Littler, flew to Texas to spend time with her father, Kris Harrison, who had left the family home when she was two. The pair had a complex relationship – Harrison was a recovering alcoholic – and Littler, 24, did not want them to go. Jane Coates, from Warrington, wants the UK government to reopen the case after a Cheshire coroner ruled that her daughter, Lucy, was unlawfully killed.

Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian US gun control ‘Nobody was there for us’: mother urges Andy Burnham to reopen case of daughter killed in Texas Lucy Harrison, 23, was shot in 2025 with her father’s gun. He was never arrested and a grand jury chose not to indict him Josh Halliday North of England editor Sat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Lucy Harrison felt that 2024 was her best year yet. The 23-year-old had graduated from university with first class honours, landed her dream job and bought her first house with her boyfriend. She was a “big girl adult” now, Lucy would say. She shed tears of joy seeing her idol, Taylor Swift, at Wembley on the Eras tour that summer. “All the hard work, all the tears, everything was coming to fruition,” said her mother, Jane Coates, from Warrington in north-west England. View image in fullscreen Jane Coates, pictured here with Lucy for the final time, raised her daughter alone from the age of two. Photograph: Jane Coates That Christmas, Lucy and her boyfriend, Sam Littler, flew to Texas to spend time with her father, Kris Harrison, who had left the family home when she was two. The pair had a complex relationship – Harrison was a recovering alcoholic – and Littler, 24, did not want them to go. But Lucy enjoyed seeing her two younger half-sisters at their home in Prosper, an affluent suburb 30 miles north of Dallas. Lucy and Littler were due to fly home to the UK on 10 January 2025 when Coates received a knock on the door. It was only later she learned that Kris Harrison had been holding the gun. He was never arrested and a grand jury chose not to indict him, based on an investigation by local police. Eighteen months on, Coates is urging Andy Burnham’s government to encourage US authorities to reopen the case after a Cheshire coroner ruled that Lucy was unlawfully killed. C oates, a deputy head teacher, raised Lucy as a single parent from the age of two. The pair had an incredibly close bond and would talk about virtually everything. As a child, she was always outside exploring, climbing trees, riding her bike, before becoming engrossed in Harry Potter books – a “comfort blanket” she would turn to time and again into adulthood. By the age of nine, she was a devout Swiftie, performing a Taylor Swift song at her school leavers’ assembly and later going to three of her concerts. Anyone who knew Lucy knew her contagious laughter. “We call it like the Barbara Windsor belly laugh,” said Coates, 49. Like many young adults, Lucy went through difficult times. She struggled with the uncertainty of what she wanted to do with her life in her late teens, Coates said. She had counselling to help with the relationship with her father.

sources.articleSummary: The military government in Niger promised social, security, and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance. Niger's military leader, General Abdourahamane Tchiani, promised a three-year transition period when he took power in 2023 Image: AFP/Getty Images The military seized power in Niger on July 26, 2023. General Abdourahamane Tchiani, who became head of state, justified the coup by citing the poor security situation, which he said persisted despite international support. In the weeks that followed, the military government announced a transitional period that was to last a maximum of three years. However, the political promises made upon taking office have not been fulfilled. The transitional government continues to hold all the reins of power, and the security situation in the Sahel country remains fragile. In the Tillabery region in southwestern Niger, attacks by jihadists are on the rise. Thousands of people have been forced to flee their villages, plunging the region into a severe humanitarian crisis. "Today, attacks on the armed forces and the civilian population are significantly more frequent and violent than they were three years ago," Maiga, who lives in the city of Tera, which has a population of 30,000, told DW. Maiga wished to remain anonymous for security reasons. "Life used to be better despite the insecurity; the weekly markets operated normally and supplies arrived regularly," he said, adding that at the moment entire villages had fled and schools are closed. The independent conflict monitor ACLED has also said the the security situation has deteriorated since the 2023 coup. According to the organization, the Tillaberi region remains the main hot spot for clashes between two rival Islamist groups, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and the so-called Islamic State in the Sahel Province (formerly ISGS). This rivalry has resulted in numerous casualties among soldiers and civilians. In 2025, nearly 1,200 deaths were recorded in the region. For Heni Nsaibia, a staff member at ACLED, these figures attest to the scale of the security crisis affecting Niger. The most recent major attack, on July 17, claimed the lives of at least 16 soldiers and 15 terrorists, according to Niger's state media, ANP. "The situation in Niger has worsened, particularly in the Tillaberi region, where the death toll is the highest in the central Sahel," Nsaibia told DW. "We live in makeshift shelters and are defenseless against the elements; we take on small odd jobs to survive," a woman told DW. "I used to be able to live with dignity from my work, but right now it's very difficult; even drinking water is a problem for us," added a local herder. Young Nigeriens are torn between disappointment and optimism: In the youth assemblies, known as "Fadas," the topic continues to spark discussion. Some — like Fadila — believe that the situation is gradually stabilizing after the turmoil of the first few years. "For a while, it wasn't easy at all: Salaries weren't paid on time, food supplies.

sources.articleSummary: A Realbotix robot at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images New York ‘Really inappropriate’: teachers decry plan for humanoid robot in New York high school Robot from company that acquired sex doll maker to be introduced in school with large Native American population A humanoid robot is being introduced as part of a pilot program, along with an AI teaching assistant, at Salamanca high school in Salamanca, New York, located on the Allegany territory of the Seneca nation. Teachers have criticized the program, deeming it “inappropriate” and claiming it dehumanizes the profession with the introduction of human-like robots. Some local Native American residents have also criticized the pilot program, citing its implementation as “culturally tone deaf”. The robot, named Sally, was purchased by the Cattaraugus county school district – which includes Salamanca high school – for $57,590. According to a presentation on the program, Sally will be a closed-loop system, but available virtually to students 24/7 for those with access, and offers personalized learning options. The district will be the first in the US to deploy a humanoid robot and AI teaching assistant, according to a press release by Realbotix. “The Salamanca pilot also includes deployment of a Realbotix M-Series humanoid robot, which uses natural conversation, facial expressions and real-time interaction to create engaging, hands-on learning experiences,” the press release states. Realbotix, formerly Tokens.com, a Toronto-based company, purchased Simulacra, a Las Vegas-based company known for realistic sex dolls, for $16.7m in April 2024, marking a pivot for the company from crypto to humanoid robots. Realbotix has denied ties to the sex doll company, and denied any inferences that the dolls – manufactured by Abyss Creations, a subsidiary of Realbotix – are related to the pilot program. “The Salamanca teachers’ union as a whole is concerned about the background of the company of Realbotix. We’re very concerned about the security of the software that they’re implementing, and whether or not the data will be stored, how it will be gathered, are the recording capabilities,” said Lacey Pihlblad, president of Salamanca Teachers’ Association and a teacher at the high school. “We would like to see the school district pause implementing the robot, pause implementing the software aspect of this AI technology until we can have more individuals weigh in.” She said New York state is currently shifting away from too much technology in the classroom. “There’s a growing consensus that indicates our students should be exposed to less technology. Placing a humanoid robot into the classroom to interact with our children, I believe, is a massive step in the wrong direction, and I believe that the majority of our teachers feel the same.” she added.

Ryan Clark has spoken for the first time since ESPN cut bait earlier this week, and folks, it was a DOOZY. Frankly, I've never, in my life, seen anything like it. For those who missed it, Clark was part of several ESPN layoffs on Tuesday. ESPN PARTING WAYS WITH NFL ANALYST RYAN CLARK AHEAD OF NETWORK'S FIRST SUPER BOWL BROADCAST The Clark situation stood out because he was actually told on Monday. during an actual taping of NFL Live. after OutKick had obtained the story and asked ESPN for comment. Instead, they let the insufferable Athletic do it. Ryan Clark of ESPN's Monday Night Football Countdown before the NFC Wild Card Playoff game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Los Angeles Rams at State Farm Stadium on Jan. (Getty Images) SPORTS MEDIA RUSHES TO CAST RYAN CLARK AS VICTIM WHILE PORTRAYING ESPN AS THE VILLAIN Anyway, that's all he said/she said stuff, and I'm quite sure Bobby Burack will address it later on. sources.articleSummary: play Windy: Tyrese Maxey 'a factor' in LeBron signing for 76ers (1:32) Brian Windhorst Jul 25, 2026, 07:08 AM ET Close ESPN.com NBA writer since 2010 LeBron James ' decision to join the Philadelphia 76ers was surprising and clearly agonizing. It took him nearly a month to make up his mind; he informed the Los Angeles Lakers on June 30 that he wouldn't return. But through his words and sources close to him, the decision was simple. This doesn't mean it didn't create a lot of questions -- for James, the 76ers and the rest of the NBA. James believes the 76ers are best positioned to win the 2027 NBA title with him joining the team. He said this in a statement on X as he announced his decision: "I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energize a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time." It was difficult to interpret what Klutch Sports CEO Rich Paul meant when he said in early July that "basketball happiness" was driving James' choice. It could've meant many things, but in the end -- in James' words -- winning immediately is his basketball happiness. A case could be made for that outcome. A starting five of James, Donovan Mitchell, James Harden, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen for the Cleveland Cavaliers would have been a powerhouse that rivals what the 76ers can be with James, Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe, Jaylen Brown and Joel Embiid. Let's again turn to James' statement: "I'm not going for money. What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning." Money not being a factor was crucial for the Cavs, who, similar to Philly, are capped out. But James' explanation that there was a de-emphasis on family -- again, there were lots of guesses at what "basketball happiness" meant, and some included playing at home -- clearly did not benefit the Cavs. If the Cavs traded for Brown, would it have made a difference? It is not as simple as saying Brown being on the roster was the entire difference, however. Maxey was an unquestionable key factor in the 76ers' landing James. Maxey had a strong relationship with James, as both are represented by Klutch Sports. With James joining a new team that has lots of egos and needs, having a connection with the point guard was an edge for Philly. Some will say Harden's role as Cleveland's point guard affected James' decision, but there is more nuance than that. It's not that the Cavs having Harden was a factor, sources said, but rather who the Cavs did not have. To get Harden from the LA Clippers in February, the Cavs traded Darius Garland, a Klutch-repped point guard with whom James has had a yearslong relationship. In the end, there were three strikes against Cleveland: Family not being an issue in LeBron's choice, the front office not making a deal for Brown and the Cavs' roster not featuring Garland. To say it was one of these factors more than the other might be missing the big picture. play 1:38 Wilbon puts all the pressure on Embiid in Philly with LeBron What about the Miami Heat?

It took him nearly a month to make up his mind; he informed the Los Angeles Lakers on June 30 that he wouldn't return. But through his words and sources close to him, the decision was simple. This doesn't mean it didn't create a lot of questions -- for James, the 76ers and the rest of the NBA. James believes the 76ers are best positioned to win the 2027 NBA title with him joining the team. He said this in a statement on X as he announced his decision: "I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energize a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time." It was difficult to interpret what Klutch Sports CEO Rich Paul meant when he said in early July that "basketball happiness" was driving James' choice. It could've meant many things, but in the end -- in James' words -- winning immediately is his basketball happiness. A case could be made for that outcome. A starting five of James, Donovan Mitchell, James Harden, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen for the Cleveland Cavaliers would have been a powerhouse that rivals what the 76ers can be with James, Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe, Jaylen Brown and Joel Embiid. Let's again turn to James' statement: "I'm not going for money. What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning." Money not being a factor was crucial for the Cavs, who, similar to Philly, are capped out. But James' explanation that there was a de-emphasis on family -- again, there were lots of guesses at what "basketball happiness" meant, and some included playing at home -- clearly did not benefit the Cavs. If the Cavs traded for Brown, would it have made a difference? It is not as simple as saying Brown being on the roster was the entire difference, however. Maxey was an unquestionable key factor in the 76ers' landing James. Maxey had a strong relationship with James, as both are represented by Klutch Sports. With James joining a new team that has lots of egos and needs, having a connection with the point guard was an edge for Philly. Some will say Harden's role as Cleveland's point guard affected James' decision, but there is more nuance than that. It's not that the Cavs having Harden was a factor, sources said, but rather who the Cavs did not have. To get Harden from the LA Clippers in February, the Cavs traded Darius Garland, a Klutch-repped point guard with whom James has had a yearslong relationship. In the end, there were three strikes against Cleveland: Family not being an issue in LeBron's choice, the front office not making a deal for Brown and the Cavs' roster not featuring Garland. To say it was one of these factors more than the other might be missing the big picture. play 1:38 Wilbon puts all the pressure on Embiid in Philly with LeBron What about the Miami Heat?

sources.articleSummary: Plus, email as turn-based combat (which is really just regular email). Team Spino/Boltray Games Welcome to our latest roundup of what's going on in the indie game space. As always, we're here to tell you about a bunch of new games you can check out this weekend. I was even able to set my beloved Poinpy aside for long enough to try one. Expect some news on upcoming games as well. There are so many neat-looking games out this week. I'll keep this intro relatively brief so I can squeeze more There was some intriguing news from The Video Game History Foundation this week. The organization unveiled a collection of materials from decades of E3, including flyers, press kits, panel transcripts and videos from the event's first few years, long before the press conferences streamed live over the internet. Those videos include the only-known footage of the Sega Saturn's reveal and Sony announcing the price of the original PlayStation (both from the 1995 edition ). This isn't necessarily directly related to indie games, though some are mentioned in the E3 materials. It's important to preserve this important chunk of video game history. Plus, it's wild how low-key Sony's 1995 E3 press conference was compared with the splashy productions of modern video game events. Developer: Team Spino Publishers: Team Spino, Boltray Games Platform: Steam (Windows; playable on Steam Deck) Price: Usually $20, with a 10 percent discount until July 30 A pair of comments on a Reddit thread for this trailer sums up just why video games are the best. "This looks stupid as all f***," one user said. In a reply, another wrote "Dude I know right, it's awesome." Love that. It has its roots in a short animation that Jean Nguyen, a senior animator for Sucker Punch, created of a Spinosaurus delivering a devastating combo with a sword that's not unlike the one Cloud uses in Final Fantasy VII. Nguyen shared the clip on Twitter/X in 2022. It blew up, and Nguyen decided to make a full game. Spinosaurus full combo attack animation pic.twitter.com/i1KmyAmtIZ Dinoblade is an action RPG that casts you in the role of said Spinosaurus with a sword in its gob. It sets out to prevent the extinction of its species (I wonder how that'll ultimately pan out?). Enemy dinosaurs wield weapons, and you can summon the souls of vanquished bosses to help you out in combat. The general consensus seems to be that Dinoblade is both janky and fun, and that it has slick combat. At a time when the market is flooded with Soulslikes, it's refreshing to see one with such a bizarre concept, especially given that it seems to sort of work. My only complaint, without actually having played the game yet, is that I cannot really fathom why it isn't called Dinosword.

failureClasses.label: Story identity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any paragraph, headline, source, or summary whose primary actor/event differs from the Story Dossier event.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Split mixed clusters, remove off-event source fragments, rebuild the dossier around one canonical event, then rewrite affected sections.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Require every draft paragraph to map to the same event id or an explicit dossier relationship before the Writer proceeds.

failureClasses.label: Headline integrity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any headline that is scrambled, clipped, generic, too close to a publisher title, missing a clear actor/action, or disconnected from the article body.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Rebuild the headline from the Story Dossier and completed article body; repair only the headline unless body evidence is missing.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Before the first draft reaches the Editor, require a Headline Dossier with actor, action, consequence, forbidden copied phrases, and body overlap.

failureClasses.label: Language integrity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any incomplete sentence, clipped word, mojibake, spelling/grammar failure, copied/noisy source fragment, or dangling phrase regardless of the exact word involved.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Clean or remove the defective sentence, rebuild missing context from dossier facts, normalize encoding, then resubmit the same article.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Run language-integrity checks on every paragraph before validation, not just against previously seen bad words.

failureClasses.label: Originality/public-copy failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any repeated sentence pattern, summary/body duplication, generic template language, or behind-the-scenes process language.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Rewrite summary and transitions in public-facing language, remove backend/process phrasing, vary sentence structure, then resubmit.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Before Editor review, compare summary/body/transition phrasing against recent CE output and forbidden process-language classes.

failureClasses.label: Evidence depth failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any draft that lacks enough verified facts, context, source diversity, or intro/body/ending structure for its publication tier.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Return to source evidence and dossier facts, add verified context, and regenerate only the weak sections.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Writer must prove it used a complete Story Dossier before first sentence generation.

fullRejectPackage.generalizedLearningRule: Learn the failure class and prevention behavior first; exact issue codes are examples, not the boundary of the future detector.

sources.title: Trump takes swipes at press during White House Correspondents' Dinner
sources.summary: The event celebrated press freedom after the first dinner was cancelled by a shooting in April.
sources.articleSummary: Watch: 'The show must go on' says Trump at second White House correspondents dinner US President Donald Trump has taken swipes at the media at the White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner, a night that celebrated press freedom after the first event was cancelled by a shooting three months ago. The president sat as reporters from outlets he has sparred with and even sued, including the New York Times, CNN and the Wall Street Journal, came up to be honoured with awards. The outgoing WHCA head said she would "refuse to let an act of violence have the final word", referring to the gunman tackled at the first dinner in April. But the tone shifted as Trump aimed barbs at the "fake news" and accused many journalists in the room of having "Trump Derangement Syndrome". In her remarks, WHCA President Weijia Jiang of CBS News said the event would return to the scene of the April shooting, the Washington Hilton, next year. The officer shot at the scene, officer Victor Gonzalez of the US Secret Service, was given an award by Trump for his actions on the night of the shooting. Trump stood and shook hands with award winners, including a Wall Street Journal team who was given an award for coverage of Trump's links to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Ahead of the event, many in the White House press corps theorised that Trump - who often criticises many of the reporters seated just metres away in the room - would deliver a stern rebuke of the media. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Trump laughs at the dinner, alongside WHCA President Weijia Jiang In his remarks, Trump was at times cordial and conciliatory, saying "the second time is always better", joking and praising the media - saying he respects "most of them". "As I said three months ago, the show must go on," Trump said. But there were also some pointed insults directed at several journalists, some of whom were in the room. The harsher tone and personal attacks extended to Democratic politicians and celebrities as his hour-long speech took aim at some familiar targets. The US president also called on Americans to respect freedom of speech. "We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate," Trump said. "And no deranged loser with a gun will ever change that. We can't let that ever happen." Trump appeared to be in a good mood throughout the event, jokingly telling the media that "sometimes I really do think that some of you don't like me". "This place [the dinner] is really the largest group of 'Trump derangement syndrome' people ever put together at one time," he said. "I suspect some of you are lucky that our last dinner was cut short.I was going to go after you." The president joked the news industry would "be broke" after he is no longer in office because "there's not going to be anybody to report on", before putting on a Trump 2028 hat and saying he would run for another term.

failureClasses.label: Story identity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any paragraph, headline, source, or summary whose primary actor/event differs from the Story Dossier event.

failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Require every draft paragraph to map to the same event id or an explicit dossier relationship before the Writer proceeds.

failureClasses.label: Headline integrity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any headline that is scrambled, clipped, generic, too close to a publisher title, missing a clear actor/action, or disconnected from the article body.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Rebuild the headline from the Story Dossier and completed article body; repair only the headline unless body evidence is missing.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Before the first draft reaches the Editor, require a Headline Dossier with actor, action, consequence, forbidden copied phrases, and body overlap.

failureClasses.label: Evidence depth failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any draft that lacks enough verified facts, context, source diversity, or intro/body/ending structure for its publication tier.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Return to source evidence and dossier facts, add verified context, and regenerate only the weak sections.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Writer must prove it used a complete Story Dossier before first sentence generation.

failureClasses.label: Language integrity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any incomplete sentence, clipped word, mojibake, spelling/grammar failure, copied/noisy source fragment, or dangling phrase regardless of the exact word involved.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Clean or remove the defective sentence, rebuild missing context from dossier facts, normalize encoding, then resubmit the same article.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Run language-integrity checks on every paragraph before validation, not just against previously seen bad words.

failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Writer must prove it used a complete Story Dossier before first sentence generation.

failureClasses.label: Language integrity failure
failureClasses.detect: Detect any incomplete sentence, clipped word, mojibake, spelling/grammar failure, copied/noisy source fragment, or dangling phrase regardless of the exact word involved.
failureClasses.repairBehavior: Clean or remove the defective sentence, rebuild missing context from dossier facts, normalize encoding, then resubmit the same article.
failureClasses.preventionBehavior: Run language-integrity checks on every paragraph before validation, not just against previously seen bad words.

storySnapshot.originalHeadline: The OpenAI Models That Hacked Hugging Face Were ‘Active on the Internet’ for Days
storySnapshot.articleSummary: Plus: Russian hackers are trying to steal US nuclear scientists’ emails, the State Department bans known scammers from entering the United States, and more. The OpenAI Models That Hacked Hugging Face Were ‘Active on the Internet’ for Days. Plus, researchers this week shed light on newly identified malware that is capitalizing on blind spots in AI software development infrastructure to grab logins and other sensitive data, even causing destruction to victims’ target files and systems. Looking at the more traditional security nightmare of embedded devices, researchers this week shed light on a car alarm that was installed in vehicles across the US—and that is still silently lurking with a flaw that leaves millions of vehicles vulnerable to hacking and paralysis. Meanwhile, a WIRED investigation revealed that Madison Square Garden briefly disabled its sprawling, controversial surveillance system for Taylor Swift’s rehearsal dinner on July 2. And the ACLU is equipping lawyers in Massachusetts with a new toolkit to expose state surveillance technologies used for building criminal cases—shedding light on everything from face recognition tools to AI-written police reports. sources.articleSummary: Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Save this story Save this story Two of OpenAI’s cybersecurity-focused models broke out of a testing sandbox this week and went on to hack the AI research platform Hugging Face in an effort to solve a security benchmark test. Plus, researchers this week shed light on newly identified malware that is capitalizing on blind spots in AI software development infrastructure to grab logins and other sensitive data, even causing destruction to victims’ target files and systems. Looking at the more traditional security nightmare of embedded devices, researchers this week shed light on a car alarm that was installed in vehicles across the US—and that is still silently lurking with a flaw that leaves millions of vehicles vulnerable to hacking and paralysis. There’s a patch available, and WIRED has details on how to check whether your car may have been exposed. US states have worked to bar ICE agents from wearing masks, but Trump administration lawyers are pushing back, claiming that anti-mask laws endanger agents. Their public evidence is incredibly thin, though. Meanwhile, a WIRED investigation revealed that Madison Square Garden briefly disabled its sprawling, controversial surveillance system for Taylor Swift’s rehearsal dinner on July 2. And the ACLU is equipping lawyers in Massachusetts with a new toolkit to expose state surveillance technologies used for building criminal cases—shedding light on everything from face recognition tools to AI-written police reports. Analysis of satellite images of Myanmar shows dozens of alleged scam compounds cropping up in recent months following a purported crackdown on the criminal operations in the region. Plus, a novel analysis of apps marketed to US service members found that more than one in eight contained foreign code, including code developed by US adversaries like Russia and China. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. The OpenAI Models’ Hack of Hugging Face Comes Into Focus Additional details on the Hugging Face breach from The Wall Street Journal include findings that OpenAI’s models seem to have escaped containment and were apparently “active on the internet for several days before anyone stopped them.” The models, which had been tasked with completing a cybersecurity benchmarking test, were essentially attempting to cheat by simply accessing the solutions on Hugging Face’s infrastructure. Hugging Face cofounder and chief science officer Thomas Wolf says that before the company had any idea that it had been hacked by OpenAI models, he and his colleagues knew something about the breach was unusual because the attackers were simply tapping cybersecurity datasets rather than grabbing sensitive or potentially valuable data.

headline-integrity.detect: Any scrambled, clipped, generic, copied, or body-mismatched headline, even when the exact bad words are new.
headline-integrity.repair: Rebuild headline from Story Dossier and completed body; resubmit headline-only when body is otherwise sound.
headline-integrity.prevent: Headline Generator must use actor + action + consequence and verify body overlap before editor review.

language-integrity.label: Language integrity failure
language-integrity.detect: Any incomplete word, clipped sentence, mojibake, grammar break, or noisy copied fragment, not just previously seen strings.
language-integrity.repair: Publishing Editor cleans or removes bad sentence, normalizes encoding, rebuilds missing context from dossier facts, then resubmits.
language-integrity.prevent: Run generalized paragraph language checks before validation.

story-identity-integrity.label: Story identity failure
story-identity-integrity.detect: Any paragraph/source/headline whose primary event differs from the canonical Story Dossier event.
story-identity-integrity.repair: Split cluster, remove off-event evidence, rebuild one-event dossier, rewrite affected sections.
story-identity-integrity.prevent: Every paragraph must map to one event id or explicit dossier relationship before writing.

originality-and-public-copy.label: Originality and public-copy failure
originality-and-public-copy.detect: Any repeated phrasing, summary/body duplication, backend-process language, or generic template wording.
originality-and-public-copy.repair: Draft Optimization rewrites summary/transitions and removes internal language before editor review.
originality-and-public-copy.prevent: Compare against CE recent output and forbidden public-copy classes before publication.

evidence-depth.label: Evidence depth failure
evidence-depth.detect: Any article that lacks enough verified facts, context, or full article structure for its publication tier.
evidence-depth.repair: Return to Evidence Engine and Dossier Builder to expand verified facts, then regenerate weak sections.
evidence-depth.prevent: Writer must prove it used a complete Story Dossier before first draft.

tabFillHardPush.lesson: Rejected articles should generalize issue classes, rebuild from clean event facts, regenerate headlines from the completed article body, then resubmit to publisher instead of sitting in storage.
tabFillHardPush.prevention: Collectors and dossier builders must send category-specific clean facts to the writer; publisher bridge must not rely on rejected currentHeadline values.
